The truth was, my own mind had become a wider and more varied country; in the ten years since my departure, I had known struggles so much more pressing than any this house could impose—joys and sorrows so much more real had shaped me than any of the cold lessons I had learned within its walls—that its oppressive stillness gave me no sense of returning dread.

“He is in the library,” the housekeeper said, her face a mask of professional apathy. “He asked that you be sent in directly.”

“Very well,” I answered, “but I should like a moment to compose myself. If you would show me to a sitting room, I should be grateful.”

The woman hesitated, her duty warring with the unexpected request. “Mr. Croft does not like to be kept waiting,” she remarked, her tone implying that this fact ought to govern all my actions. I simply met her gaze, and after a moment she turned and led me to a small, cold parlour. I removed my hat and smoothed my hair, uninvited, and told her I would find my own way to the library when I was ready. I did not go at once; instead, I sought out the old cook, Mrs. Gable, in her kitchens, and took a cup of tea, and heard from her the true state of the master’s health. It had been my way, formerly, to obey any summons from Mr. Croft with trembling haste: received as I had been to-day, I should, a decade ago, have flown to his side in a panic of apprehension; now, it was revealed to me with absolute clarity that my time was my own. I had travelled from the city at his behest, a summons I had almost ignored, and I would see him; but not as a frightened ward, but as a woman who had earned her own bread and her own peace.

So I made my way to the library; I needed no guide to that well-remembered chamber, to which I had so often been called for correction and intellectual dissection in my formative years. I pushed open the heavy oak door: a scent of dry paper and leather met me, unchanged. There was the vast desk of polished mahogany, as of old; there the towering shelves, the rolling ladder, and the globe, upon whose surface I had a hundred times been forced to trace the campaigns of conquerors, to account for errors of geography I had not made. I glanced towards a particular wing-backed chair, half-expecting to see the ghost of a small, pale girl sitting there, her hands clasped tight in her lap, waiting for the inevitable pronouncement of her inadequacy. I approached the fireplace; I set my hand on the cold marble mantel and leaned my head against it. It is a strange mercy that experience wears away the sharp edges of resentment and softens the bitterest recollections. I had fled this man in anguish and defiance, and I returned to him now with no stronger feeling than a kind of sober curiosity for his decline, and a faint desire to understand and be understood; to close the account and be at peace.

The well-known figure was there: frail, diminished, but arrogant as ever—there was that piercing eye which nothing could soften, and the thin, sardonic lip. How often had it curled with disdain at my tentative opinions! and how the memory of my girlhood’s anxieties and humiliations resurfaced as I saw him now! And yet I walked towards him and held out my hand. He looked at it, then at me.

“Is this Eleanor Vance?” he said.

“Yes, Mr. Croft. I came as soon as I could.” I had once promised myself that I would never again stand in his presence: I felt no compunction in breaking that promise now. My eyes had met his, and I waited for some sign of recognition, of connection. Had he offered me his hand warmly, I should at that moment have felt a genuine gladness. “You have been long in coming,” he remarked, his voice thin as paper. Again he examined me so critically, I perceived at once that his estimation of me—his conviction of my mediocrity—was unchanged and unchangeable. I knew by his flinty gaze—impervious to sentiment, insoluble by kindness—that he was resolved to find me wanting to the last; because to believe me his equal would offer him no satisfaction: only a sense of his own judgment being flawed. I felt a prick of old pain, and then a surge of indignation; and then I felt a resolution to master the situation—to be the mistress of my own mind in spite of his will. My throat had tightened, just as in childhood: I consciously relaxed it. I did not take the stool, but brought a proper chair and sat opposite him.

“You sent for me,” I said, “and I am here; and it is my wish to know why.”

“Oh, certainly! You have made a life for yourself, I hear?”

“I have.”

“Well, you may tell your patrons that I have a matter to discuss with you. To-night I am fatigued, and I find my thoughts wander. Frowning, he shifted in his chair; my gaze, resting on a pile of books at his elbow, held steady: he was at once annoyed.

“Attend to me!” said he. “Are you Eleanor Vance?”

I declare she once argued with me about Plato, like some half-taught governess—no pupil ever presumed to argue as she did; I was relieved when she left my house. What did they teach you in that school you attended? The Brontë sisters, I suppose, and other such hysterics. She, however, did not fail: but I always said she would—I wish she had!”

“A singular wish, Mr. Croft; why did you resent her so?”

You have given me back a part of my own soul, and that is a thing your reason can no longer take from me.”

The letters. There were perhaps a dozen of them, the ink a rusty brown, the penmanship elegant and sloping. I opened the first. It was dated a month before his death.

“My Dearest Eleanor,” it began. “If you read this, it is because I am gone, and you are left in the care of my cousin, a man whose mind I respect but whose heart I fear. He believes feeling is a sickness of the soul. I believe it is the soul itself.”

I had my legacy. It was not written in Latin or in Greek; it was written in love, and it was mine.

The accusation in his voice was raw, possessive. A year ago, it might have frightened or angered me. Now, it only filled me with a strange, aching tenderness. His love for me had not been dimmed by time or tragedy; it was as fierce and demanding as ever.

The injustice of his words struck me, but I quelled the rising heat of my indignation. I saw his cruelty for what it was: the desperate lashing out of a proud man in profound pain, a man who believed himself unworthy, unlovable. He was testing me, pushing me away to see if I would go.

A thousand miles away, in a quiet room, I heard your voice call my name. I heard you in despair, and I came. I would have come had I been a beggar. My fortune is of no consequence, except that it makes me my own mistress. And as my own mistress, I have chosen my course. I have come back to you.”

He turned his head towards me again, his unseeing eyes wide. “You heard me? What is this fantasy?”

“His proposal!” Rochester broke in, the word a snarl. “The clergyman’s!”

You must go out into the world and find a husband worthy of you. Someone whole. Someone who can see your face when you smile.”

He was trying to send me away for my own good, just as he had tried once before on a sunny garden bench at Thornfield. But I was not the same girl. I was no longer a dependant, swayed by his moods and his commands. I was a woman, his equal, and I would not be dismissed.

The word hung in the air between us, momentous and terrifying and beautiful. He flinched as if I had struck him.

Marry your cousin the clergyman. Marry anyone. But do not sacrifice yourself on this altar of pity.”

I love you more now, in your ruin, than I ever did in your pride. I will not be sent away. I offer you my life, not as a sacrifice, but as a gift, because my life is worthless without you. I will be your eyes. I will be your hands. I will be your wife. Please, Edward. Say you will have me. Ask me to marry you.”

“Ask you?” he said, his voice choked. “I, who am not fit to be your servant, ask you to be my wife?”

“Yes,” I whispered, leaning in close, my tears falling on his face. “Ask me. I want to hear you ask me.”

Pilot rested his great head on my master’s knee. Finally, he lifted his hand and cupped the back of my head, his fingers tangling in my hair.

We were no longer master and governess, no longer a rich man and a poor dependant. We were two souls, long parted, who had found their way back to one another, and who would, from that moment on, be one. I would be his eyes, and he would be my world.

“My small Jane,” he breathed. “My good fairy. I thought you had forsaken this world for one of your own, a realm of spirits and starlight. And yet you come back to a cripple in a desolate house.”

“Ferndean is not desolate now,” I said, my voice gaining a firmness I was pleased to feel. “And you are not a cripple; you are my Edward. The same man I have always known, and always loved.”

A sound, half-laugh, half-groan, escaped his lips. “Always loved? You loved my pride, Jane, my strength. What is there to love now?”

“I love the soul,” I answered, “which neither fire nor misfortune can destroy. I love the heart that called for me across the moors. Do you think so little of me, that I can only love what is whole and perfect in the world’s eyes? My love is not so poor a thing as that.”

He was silent, but his hand tightened on mine. The fire, which had been our only companion and light, was now sinking into a dull red glow. A chill began to creep into the room. It was the intrusion of the prosaic, the necessary world, reminding us that even the most sublime moments must yield to the practical demands of life.

“The fire is dying,” I said quietly. “And you are cold. John’s wife, Mary, should she not come and build it up?”

“Let it die,” he said, a note of his old peremptoriness in his tone. “I have no need of it. You are here; you are my warmth and my light.”

“That may be poetry, sir, but it is not sense,” I returned, with a hint of Bessie’s practicality in my own voice. “You will take a chill, and I shall have to play the nurse in earnest. I will call for Mary.”

I made to rise, but he held my hand fast. “Stay. Do not leave me yet. Not for a moment. Let Mary come in her own time. Tell me, Jane, tell me of your year. Tell me everything. I would know every step you have taken since you fled from me like a startled bird.”

And so I sat, there in the gathering darkness, and began my tale. I spoke of my wanderings, of my near starvation, and of the blessed providence that led me to the door of my cousins. I told him of St. John, of his cold zeal and his proposal; I confessed it all, for there could be no secrets between us now. He listened without interruption, his face a mask of shadows, his hand a constant, firm pressure on mine. When I spoke of St. John’s offer of marriage, his fingers tightened until they were almost painful, and a low growl rumbled in his chest, a sound I remembered well.

“He dared?” he muttered. “That pillar of ice, that marble saint? He presumed to ask for my Jane, to take you to the ends of the earth to perish in his shadow? God forgive me, but I am glad I cannot see him; I should be tempted to do him a violence.”

“He is a good man, in his way,” I said, wishing to be just. “But his way was not, and could never be, mine. My heart was always here, at Thornfield, or wherever you might be.”

“And the fortune, Jane? The twenty thousand pounds? You did not mention that. Are you an heiress now?” There was a peculiar note in his voice, a mixture of wonder and a new kind of distance.

“It is five thousand pounds,” I corrected him. “I gave the rest to my cousins, who needed it and deserved it. It is enough. It is more than enough for us.” I stressed the final word, wanting him to understand at once.

“For us?” he repeated slowly. “Jane, that money is yours. This ruin is mine. Do not confuse the two. I will not live on your charity. I am not a pauper to be kept by his wife.”

Here it was, then: the pride I had both admired and feared, the very core of his nature, reasserting itself even in his broken state. I knew this was a delicate and perilous moment; a single misstep on my part could wound him more deeply than any physical blow. I chose my words with the utmost care.

“It is not charity, Edward. It is a sharing. When I was a penniless governess, you offered me your name, your home, your wealth, without a moment’s thought for the disparity. Did I feel then that I was accepting charity? No; I felt I was being given the kingdom of heaven. Now, our positions are, in the world’s small view, somewhat reversed. It is my turn to bring what I have to our union. It is our fortune now, as all that you have, this house, this land, will be our home. We are to be one flesh; shall we not also be one purse?”

I felt the tension in him lessen, the rigid set of his shoulders soften. He brought my hand to his lips and kissed it, not with passion, but with a kind of reverent gratitude. “My Jane,” he said, his voice thick with emotion. “You have an answer for everything. You have a logic that silences even my own stubborn pride. Forgive me; I am not used to this new territory of dependence. I shall stumble often.”

“And I will be there to offer my arm,” I replied. “We shall learn to walk this new path together.”

Just then, a shuffling sound was heard in the hall, followed by a light tap at the door. “That will be Mary,” I whispered, rising to my feet. “Shall I let her in?”

“Yes,” he said, composing his features. “The world must be faced, I suppose.”

I opened the door to a stout, middle-aged woman with a kind, anxious face. It was John’s wife. She carried a tray with a single candle and a bowl of what I presumed was gruel. She started upon seeing me, her eyes widening in surprise.

“Beg pardon, sir,” she said, her gaze flickering from me to her master. “I did not know you had a visitor. John said naught.”

“This is Miss Eyre, Mary,” Mr. Rochester said, his voice calm and steady. “She has done me the honour of coming to see me. She will be staying.”

“Staying, sir?” Mary looked from me, to the single chair, to the dying embers in the grate, a world of questions in her simple, honest face.

“Yes, staying,” he repeated. “For the rest of her life, if I have my way. She has consented to be my wife.”

Mary’s jaw dropped. The bowl of gruel tilted precariously. I reached out and steadied her hand, a faint smile touching my lips. “It is true, Mary,” I said. “Do not spill the master’s supper on account of it.”

The woman’s face broke into a wide, incredulous grin. “His wife? Oh, sir! Oh, miss! This is the best news this sad house has heard in a year! The very best news! Oh, praise be!” She set the tray down with a clatter, her hands trembling with excitement, and wiped a tear from her eye with the corner of her apron. “A mistress for Ferndean! And such a one as you, miss. I remember you from Thornfield, a quiet little thing, but with a good heart, I always said.”

“Thank you, Mary,” I said, genuinely touched by her simple, heartfelt welcome. It was the first benediction upon our union, and it meant more to me than a bishop’s blessing.

“You will need a room prepared, miss,” she bustled, all efficiency now. “The green chamber is the least damp, though heaven knows none of them have been aired proper for months. I’ll see to it at once. I’ll have John bring up your trunk. You have a trunk, I suppose?”

“It is at the inn in Millcote,” I replied. “I walked the last few miles.”

“Walked!” Mary exclaimed, horrified. “All that way, and in this weather! The master must send John for it on the morrow. Tonight, you shall have to make do. I can find you a nightdress, and I’ll put a warming pan in the bed myself.”

Her practical solicitude was a comfort, grounding us in the reality of the coming night and the days to follow. While she went to see to my room, I returned to Mr. Rochester’s side. I took the bowl of gruel from the tray.

“You must eat,” I said, taking a spoon. “You are weak.”

He made a face. “I detest gruel. It is the food of invalids and infants.”

“And you are, for the moment, an invalid,” I said firmly. “And I shall treat you as an infant if you are not sensible. Open your mouth.”

A flicker of a smile, the ghost of his old, teasing self, crossed his lips. He sighed in mock surrender. “Very well, my tyrant. But only because you command it. It seems I have exchanged one master, my own will, for another, far more formidable one: a slip of a girl with a determined chin.”

I fed him the gruel, spoonful by spoonful, as I might have fed a child. There was no sense of degradation in the act, either for him or for me; it was simply a service of love, a necessary act of care. He, who had once bestrode the world like a colossus, was now dependent upon me for the simplest of sustenance, and yet, in this very dependence, I felt our souls were more truly equal than they had ever been. When the bowl was empty, I set it aside and wiped his lips with a napkin.

“Now,” I said. “It is late. You should sleep.”

“And you?” he asked, his hand finding mine in the gloom.

“Mary is preparing a room for me. I shall be just down the hall. I will not be far.”

“Do not go yet,” he pleaded, his voice losing its forced lightness. “The darkness is deeper when I know you are near, yet not with me. Stay a little longer. Sing to me, Jane, as you used to. Let me hear your voice.”

I did not have a piano, as at Thornfield, but my voice was my own. I sat on a low stool beside his chair, held his hand in both of mine, and began to sing. I chose a simple Scottish air he had once professed to like, a song of home and abiding love. My voice was not powerful, but it was clear and true, and it filled the dark, silent room. He leaned his head back against the chair, his scarred face turned towards me, and I saw by the faint, residual glow of the embers that two slow, difficult tears were tracing paths down his cheeks. He did not try to hide them, and I did not pretend not to see. They were not tears of weakness or of self pity, but of a great, overwhelming, and painful joy; the tears of a man who, having thought himself damned to a perpetual night, had seen the unexpected dawn.

I sang until his breathing grew deep and even, and his hand relaxed in mine. Mary appeared at the door, a candle in her hand, and beckoned to me silently. I gently disengaged my fingers from his, tucked a blanket more securely around him, and pressed a kiss to his brow that was as light as a moth’s wing. He did not stir.

“His room is just there, miss,” Mary whispered, pointing to a door adjacent to the parlour. “He has not been able to manage the stairs since the… since it happened. But yours is ready, upstairs. The green room, as I said. It is the best we have.”

I followed her up a narrow, winding staircase, my heart a strange mixture of soaring happiness and a sober, weighty sense of responsibility. The house was even more dilapidated than I had first perceived; there was a smell of damp and decay in the air, and the wallpaper in the hall was peeling in long, sorrowful strips. The green room, however, was clean. A fire had been lit in the small grate, casting a cheerful, dancing light on the walls, and the bed, with its faded green hangings, looked surprisingly inviting. A simple, worn nightdress was laid out upon the quilt.

“It’s not what you’d be used to, I’m sure, miss,” Mary said apologetically. “Not after Mr. Rivers’s fine house.”

“It is perfect, Mary,” I assured her. “It is home.”

She smiled, pleased. “I’ll bring you some hot water in the morning. Good night, miss. And… welcome.”

“Good night, Mary. And thank you.”

When she had gone, I went to the window and looked out. There was no moon; the darkness was absolute. I could see nothing of the grounds, but I could hear the soughing of the wind in the trees, a lonely, ancient sound. A year ago, this house, this darkness, this isolation, would have filled me with a nameless dread. Tonight, it felt like a sanctuary. The grand edifice of Thornfield had been a place of secrets and shadows, of a hidden madness that had nearly consumed us all. This humble, decaying manor was a place of honesty. There were no more secrets. The madness had been exorcised by fire, the pride had been washed clean by suffering. What was left was the truth, stark and difficult, but the truth nonetheless.

I had found my place. I was no longer a restless spirit, a solitary wanderer. I was Jane Rochester, not yet in name, but in heart and soul and unbreakable purpose. I would be his eyes, his hands, his guide in the darkness. I would restore his world, not by grand gestures, but by the steady, daily application of love and care. I would read to him from his books, walk with him in his woods, describe to him the changing of the seasons. I would fill this desolate house with life and light, and I would cherish the broken man I loved more fiercely than I had ever cherished the proud master. It was a great and daunting task, but my heart did not quail. It sang with a quiet, profound, and unshakeable joy. Reader, I was home.
